newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan money policy firm despite slow M2.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan money policy firm despite slow M2.

text.p: Taiwan's lower-than-expected May M2 money supply growth points to a slack recovery, but analysts said on Wednesday the central bank was unlikely to loosen monetary policy -- lest the red-hot stock market overheat.
M2, Taiwan's broadest money supply measure, grew just 8.99 percent in May from a year earlier, the central bank said on Wednesday.

The rise was the first time M2 had fallen below the central bank's 9-14 percent target zone since December, just before the bank adopted a broader definition that economists said added one to 1.5 percentage points to the key indicator.
M2 growth was well below an average 9.438 percent forecast compiled from a June 23 Reuters poll of Taiwan economists.
Despite the disappointing rise, experts said Taiwan's economic situation leaves monetary policymakers handcuffed.

"The slow M2 growth indicates a slow economic recovery, but the central bank is unlikely to loosen its monetary policy because of concerns over the rallying stock market," said HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang, whose 9.0 forecast in the Reuters Poll was closest to the actual figure.

"Any further loosening of monetary policy would merely flush funds into the stock market or trigger capital outflows, rather than lead to actual investment that would boost the economy as a looser policy is supposed to do," Wang said.
The central bank attributed the low money supply rise mainly to slowing growth in bank loans and investments and a major rise in government deposits.

M2 also sagged on the central bank's unusually high issuance of negotiable certificates of deposit in May and a temporary tightening of liquidity at the peak of the treasury's annual income tax collection, economists said.

Economists said fears of chilling Taiwan's recovery were likely to check any central bank inclinations to tighten monetary policy, despite worries that loose liquidity, rather than fundamental equity, was driving share prices higher.
"In view of the slow recovery and hot stock market, the central bank likely will keep its current stable-to-loose, but not-too-loose, policy," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
The stock index closed on Wednesday at another seven-year high, gaining 38.24 points or 0.43 percent to 8,956.41.
Share prices have rocketed some 12 percent since late May.

So frantic has the stock market been in recent days that it has sucked funds from the banking system, driving the interbank overnight rate briefly above nine percent -- a 21-month high on Tuesday -- and halting what had been a steady depreciation of the Taiwan dollar as investors dumped U.S. dollars to raise investable cash.

The central bank has said it would tinker with liquidity through issues of negotiable certificates of deposit, but vowed not to inject funds through open-market operations despite the liquidity squeeze.

Central bank banking unit chief Lee Sheng-yen, in comments late on Tuesday, added that the bank did not plan to cut banks' reserve requirements because "the current tight liquidity will not last long".
The central bank has said it would cut reserve requirements by the end of 1997 in line with international trends.
Analysts predict the move will stoke the stock market and even without such a cut predict a firming trend for the stock market, seeing it testing 9,500 points in the near term.

"I believe the stock market will remain hot in the latter half because a hot stock market will help stabilise the economy and prevent capital from flowing out, especially in view of the low interest rates and depreciating currency," Wang said.
Wang forecast the M2 growth would continue to slow, drifting toward eight percent in the second half, eventually forcing the central bank to adjust its 9-13 percent M2 target.
"Slow money demand likely will force the central bank to lower its M2 growth target zone to 8-13 percent in the second half," Wang said.
